headline: A ship ran the US blockade of Iran. A plane stopped it.
summary: US Central Command said Friday that a military aircraft fired at the stern of the Pacific Archer, a Palau-flagged merchant ship, in the Gulf of Oman on Thursday. The ship had left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas and kept going after warnings. Its engine failed and the crew was unharmed. It is at least the 15th ship disabled since April.

cover_question.q: Is the war with Iran over or not?

cover_answer: Trump says effectively. Two carriers say otherwise.
table_question: If you warn someone three times and they keep going, what then?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Far away across the ocean, American warships are keeping boats from going in and out of a country called Iran. One ship tried to slip past, and an airplane shot at the back of it so its engine stopped. Nobody was hurt. It's like a goalie stopping a ball, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Only if they hear it. Nobody hurt comes first, and the goalie turns a shot into a stop. At this age they read your face before the words, so keep your voice ordinary.
5-7.why_long: Nothing to raise unprompted. If a warship is on the TV, a five-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event and reads your face before your words, so the script leads with the crew being fine and hands them a goalkeeper. Blockade means block; that is all it needs to mean today. Expect 'will they come here?' No. Far away.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Since April, US warships have blocked Iran's ports; the military says it has turned 158 ships around. On Thursday a cargo ship left Bandar Abbas and kept going after warnings, so a US aircraft fired at its stern and the engine quit. The crew was fine. Like a referee: warning, warning, then the whistle.
8-12.why: Warnings, then the engine: a rule applied in the same order each time. The referee keeps the force on the ship.
8-12.why_long: A child this age is testing whether a rule gets applied the same way each time. The chain is a blockade since April, a ship that left port anyway, warnings, then a shot at the engine, and 158 ships turned back is the rule in use. Expect 'what if it had kept going?' The article answers from June: three sailors died when a tanker was hit.

13-17.script: Is a shot at a cargo ship's engine the least force that works? This crew was warned and nobody was hurt; in June a strike like it killed three Indian sailors. Second: Trump calls the war "effectively over" while two carriers enforce a blockade that has stopped 158 ships. What does over mean?
13-17.why: Proportion first, then a word. A warned ship against June's dead, and "effectively over" against two carriers.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script asks for proportion: a warned ship and no one hurt, set against June, when a strike like it killed three sailors. Then a phrase to test, "effectively over," against two carriers still on station. Expect 'why is the war still on?' The articles don't settle it.

5-7.a: No. The plane hit the back of the ship so it couldn't move. The crew was fine.

8-12.a: Warships around a country's ports so nothing sails in or out.

8-12.q: Why shoot at the ship at all?
8-12.a: It warns the ship first, several times. Then the engine.

13-17.q: Is the war with Iran over or not?
13-17.a: Trump says effectively over. The blockade is still on.

13-17.q: Can the US just fire on a merchant ship?
13-17.a: At least 15 times since spring, in a war that began in February.
